ican.text: I can use unit-circle coordinates to interpret sine and cosine for angles in different quadrants.
I can apply $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ and $\tan\theta=\sin\theta/\cos\theta$ with their restrictions.
I can explain how the unit circle generates the sine and cosine graphs.
I can solve a trigonometric equation graphically on a finite interval and check all solutions.
I can identify and solve the ambiguous sine-rule case when two triangles are possible.

ku.text: On the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ centred at the origin, the terminal point for angle $\theta$ in standard position is $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. Positive angles turn anticlockwise from the positive $x$-axis; negative angles turn clockwise.
The identity $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ follows by substituting the unit-circle coordinates into $x^2+y^2=1$. It holds for every real angle.
$\tan\theta=\sin\theta/\cos\theta$ only where $\cos\theta\ne0$. In particular tangent is undefined at $\theta=\pi/2+k\pi$, for integer $k$.

Sine is the vertical coordinate and cosine is the horizontal coordinate. Their signs depend on the quadrant; tangent has the sign of their quotient. On an axis, use the actual coordinates rather than a quadrant mnemonic.

To obtain the sine graph, plot the vertical coordinate of the unit-circle point against the angle; cosine uses the horizontal coordinate. Each repeats after $2\pi$ radians, while tangent repeats after $\pi$ where defined.

To solve $f(x)=g(x)$ graphically on a finite interval, graph both sides in the same angle mode, choose a window showing the entire interval, and find every intersection. Include endpoints if they satisfy the equation and avoid points where a function is undefined.

When using inverse sine, the calculator returns a principal value. A supplementary angle may have the same sine. Check all relevant solutions against the stated interval and the original equation, including any excluded points.

In the ambiguous sine-rule situation, two sides and an angle opposite one of them can produce zero, one or two triangles. If $\sin B=b\sin A/a=q$ with $0<q<1$, test both $B_1=\sin^{-1}q$ and $B_2=180^\circ-B_1$. Keep only angles for which $A+B<180^\circ$.
If $q>1$ there is no real angle $B$ and hence no triangle; if $q=1$, $B=90^\circ$ is the sole candidate. For $0<q<1$, the angle-sum test decides whether one or both candidates make a triangle.

The local AI syllabus states exact trigonometric values will not be assessed, although special-angle values can illuminate the unit circle. Decimal solutions should be rounded as requested and obtained using the correct angle mode.

formula.text: Sine rule: $a/\sin A=b/\sin B=c/\sin C$, with each side opposite the corresponding angle.

worked.prompt: A point $P$ lies on the unit circle in quadrant II and has vertical coordinate $3/5$. Separately, triangle $ABC$ has $A=30^\circ$, $a=7$ cm and $b=10$ cm, where each lowercase side is opposite its corresponding uppercase angle.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ for the angle of $P$ in standard position.
parts.a: $\sin\theta=3/5$. From $x^2+(3/5)^2=1$, $x=\pm4/5$. Quadrant II has negative $x$, so $\cos\theta=-4/5$ and $\tan\theta=(3/5)/(-4/5)=-3/4$.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Solve $\sin x=0.6$ for $0\leq x\leq2\pi$, using a graph or suitable technology. Give answers to three decimal places.
parts.a: In radian mode graph $y=\sin x$ and $y=0.6$ over the whole interval. The two intersections have inputs $x\approx0.644$ and $x\approx2.498$ radians. Both endpoints have sine zero, so neither is a solution.

parts.label: c
parts.q: For triangle $ABC$, find all possible values of $B$ and $C$.
parts.a: The sine rule gives $\sin B=10\sin30^\circ/7=5/7$. In degree mode, $B_1=\sin^{-1}(5/7)\approx45.585^\circ$ and $B_2=180^\circ-B_1\approx134.415^\circ$. Both satisfy $30^\circ+B<180^\circ$. The corresponding $C$ values are $104.415^\circ$ and $15.585^\circ$, respectively.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Find the corresponding values of side $c$ and explain why there are two answers.
parts.a: For each valid triangle, $c/\sin C=7/\sin30^\circ=14$. Thus $c\approx13.6$ cm for $C\approx104.415^\circ$, or $c\approx3.76$ cm for $C\approx15.585^\circ$. The two supplementary candidates for $B$ both leave a positive angle $C$, so both triangles satisfy the given data.

parts.label: e
parts.q: State whether $\tan x$ is defined at $x=\pi/2$ and explain.
parts.a: It is undefined because $\cos(\pi/2)=0$, so $\sin x/\cos x$ would require division by zero.

kq.q: Why does the Pythagorean identity hold on the unit circle?
kq.model: The coordinates satisfy $x^2+y^2=1$. Substituting $x=\cos\theta$ and $y=\sin\theta$ gives the identity.

kq.q: Why can a sine equation have two solutions in a turn?
kq.model: Two unit-circle points can have the same vertical coordinate while having opposite horizontal coordinates. Their angles can be supplementary.

kq.q: Why do both ambiguous-case candidates need an angle-sum check?
kq.model: A supplementary angle has the same sine, but it does not necessarily leave a positive third angle in the triangle.

kq.q: Why might a graphing calculator miss a solution?
kq.model: The window, interval, angle mode or search range may hide an intersection. Inspect the entire specified interval and test endpoints and domain restrictions.
